Machine-Translate Other Responses

translate_other_responses.Rd

Fills the translation column of an other-responses data frame with an English machine translation of each response, using Google Translate's free web service. The detected language is shown in front of each translation, e.g. "[Arabic] I want to work".

Usage

translate_other_responses(
  df,
  translate = "preview",
  options = ck_translate_options(),
  verbose = TRUE
)

Arguments

df

Data frame from prepare_other_responses(). One made by an earlier version (with response_en and no translation column) also works.

translate

"preview" (the default) returns the texts that would be sent and sends nothing. TRUE sends them and fills the translation column. FALSE does nothing and returns df with an empty translation column.

options

Settings from ck_translate_options().

verbose

Logical. Print what is being sent and how it went. Default TRUE.

Value

With translate = TRUE or FALSE, df with its translation column. With translate = "preview", a data frame with one row per text that would be sent: text_to_send (exactly as it would be sent, after masking), n_responses (how many responses share it) and questions.

Details

Nothing is sent unless you ask for it. The default, translate = "preview", sends nothing: it returns the exact list of texts that would be sent, so a team can check it first. Only translate = TRUE contacts Google.

What is sent

Only the text of the "other" responses, and each distinct text once. No uuid, enumerator, date, location, question or any other column is sent, and nothing links a text to the respondent. Before sending:

  • blank responses and responses with no letters (only numbers or punctuation) are skipped;

  • long numbers are masked as ##### (see mask_numbers in ck_translate_options());

  • texts already in the cache, and rows whose translation is already filled, are skipped.

The texts travel in the body of an HTTPS request, not in the web address, so they do not end up in proxy or browser logs. Google still receives them, and it sees the computer's IP address. The free service comes with no data processing agreement: check your data-protection rules before using it.

Limits and failures

Google does not publish limits for the free service and blocks a computer that sends too much too fast. Texts are therefore combined into batches, requests are paced, and a "too many requests" reply is retried after a growing wait (see ck_translate_options()). If Google keeps refusing, sending stops. A text that could not be translated is left blank with a warning, and the rest of the work carries on; with a cache_file, run it again later and only the missing texts are sent.

Accuracy

Machine translation of short, informal, misspelt answers is often wrong, and the language of a one-word answer can be misdetected. The translation is a help for the reviewer, never applied to the data: confirm it against the original response. A response detected as English is left blank, as is one whose translation is identical to the original.

See also

ck_translate_options(), prepare_other_responses()

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# see what would be sent - nothing leaves the computer
preview <- translate_other_responses(other_responses_df)
View(preview)

# send it
other_responses_df <- translate_other_responses(
  other_responses_df,
  translate = TRUE,
  options = ck_translate_options(cache_file = "output/translation_cache.rds")
)
} # }
